title: Not many words (Matthew 6:7–8)
hook: your Father knows what you need before you ask

segments.voice: Yesterday, hupokrites, an actor behind a mask, and a prayer behind a shut door. Your line was the father sees in secret.

Some people feel they can't pray because they don't know the right words. They've heard others pray beautifully, in long flowing sentences, and they freeze. Others pray the way people write emails to someone important: carefully, at length, explaining everything, just in case. Both are asking the same question: how much do I have to say to be heard? Right after shut the door and pray in secret, Jesus answers it.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `PRAYING LIKE A LONG EMAIL.` → `HOW MUCH DO I HAVE TO SAY?`

segments.voice: When you pray, he says, don't babble on, thinking you'll be heard because of your many words. The Greek verb is battalogeo. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and nobody knows exactly where it comes from. Some scholars think it's a sound word, like blah-blah-blah: batta-batta, heaping up syllables. Then the reason, in the King James Bible: "your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." That changes what prayer is for. You're not informing God. You're not filing a report. He already knows, Jesus says. So why pray at all? Christians have long asked that, and one common answer is that prayer isn't mainly for passing on information. It's for being with someone, like a friend who sits beside you in a hospital waiting room, not to pass on news, but to be with you. A fair question: what about repeating prayers? Christians read this verse in different ways. Catholics pray the rosary, Orthodox Christians repeat the Jesus Prayer, and they say the warning is against empty words, not repeated ones. After all, in Gethsemane, Mark says Jesus "went away, and prayed, and spake the same words." Some Protestant Christians hear the verse as a caution against praying by rote, and favor praying in their own words. Both agree on the heart: it's not the number of words that reaches God. The very next thing Jesus does is teach a short prayer, and that's tomorrow.
screen: `BATTALOGEO: BLAH-BLAH-BLAH.` · `HE KNOWETH BEFORE YE ASK.` · `PRAYER: TURNING TOWARD SOMEONE.` · `EMPTY WORDS, NOT REPEATED ONES.` · then, large: `YOUR FATHER KNOWETH WHAT THINGS YE HAVE NEED OF.`

segments.voice: Think of what's weighing on you most today, and shrink it to ten words or fewer: help my mother; I'm afraid about tomorrow; thank you for this morning. If you pray, say those few words to God once, then just sit, trusting that he already knows the rest. If you don't pray, simply name it, and let the silence hold it.
Battalogeo, the Greek word for babbling on, heaping up empty words. Don't babble on to be heard; your Father knows what you need before you ask.
Your line: he already knows. What you need, before you ask him. Tomorrow, the prayer again.

howItsDone: Christians pray both in set words and in their own words: Catholics and Orthodox often use repeated prayers like the rosary and the Jesus Prayer, and many Protestants favor short spontaneous prayers; across the churches, prayer is often described as turning toward God rather than informing him.

battalogeo: rare, etymology uncertain, possibly onomatopoeic (or from Aramaic battal, 'idle'). Confirm.
